subject: Archaeology
subcategory: Lost Cities of the Ancient World
title: Ephesus: Rome's Eastern Jewel
description: A quick win: understand Ephesus: Rome's Eastern Jewel.

hook.text: Ephesus was once the second-largest city in the Roman Empire. Today it sits five miles from the sea.

buildup.text: Its library held 12,000 scrolls and its theater seated 25,000 — bigger than many modern concert venues.

discovery.text: Excavations revealed public toilets with running water, heated floors, and a medical school with surgical tools.

twist.text: The city died because the harbor silted up. Without sea access, trade vanished and people left.

climax.text: The Temple of Artemis there was one of the Seven Wonders. Only a single column remains standing today.

punchline.text: A city with heated floors and flush toilets was killed by mud.

quiz.question: What caused the decline of Ephesus?
options: A massive earthquake destroyed the city's infrastructure
The harbor silted up, cutting off sea trade
A plague wiped out most of the population

details.summary: Ephesus on Turkey's Aegean coast was one of the largest cities in the Roman Empire, with a population of over 250,000. Its marble-paved streets, Library of Celsus, enormous theater, and sophisticated plumbing demonstrate the scale and sophistication of Roman provincial urban life.
details.whyItMatters: Ephesus is the best-preserved classical city in the eastern Mediterranean. It reveals how Roman urbanism spread across the empire, transforming local communities into sophisticated cities with theaters, baths, libraries, and public services.
takeaways: One of the largest Roman cities with over 250,000 residents
Features the iconic Library of Celsus and a 25,000-seat theater
Shows the scale of Roman provincial urban development

faq.question: Why was Ephesus abandoned?
faq.answer: The harbor silted up over centuries as the Meander River deposited sediment. Without its port, the city lost its commercial purpose. The coastline retreated several kilometers, leaving Ephesus landlocked. Earthquakes and Arab raids accelerated the decline during the Byzantine period.

faq.question: What was the Library of Celsus?
faq.answer: Built around 117 CE as a monumental tomb and library, it held about 12,000 scrolls, making it the third-largest library in the Roman world. Its ornate two-story facade with allegorical statues of Wisdom, Knowledge, Intelligence, and Virtue has been reconstructed and is Ephesus's most iconic.
